Title: GitHub workflow: own account, branch, pull request, review, and a check of our repository and board
User story: As a team member, I want to practise the GitHub workflow on my own account and check our team repository and board, so that all our later work is saved, reviewed and visible. (GitHub = a website where teams keep and share code. Repository = the project folder stored on GitHub. Branch = a separate copy of the work where you can try changes safely. Pull request = a request to add your changes to the main work so teammates can review them.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I accepted the repository invite, can see the team board with all backlog items, and made one pull request that a teammate reviewed and merged.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: FastAPI hello world
User story: As a team member, I want to build a FastAPI hello world, so that I understand how our backend answers requests. (FastAPI = a Python tool for building the backend, the part that holds the logic and talks to the database. API = the way a web page asks the server for data.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) Opening the /hello address in a browser shows a message from my FastAPI program.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: React with Tailwind hello world
User story: As a team member, I want to build a React page styled with Tailwind, so that I understand how our web interface is made. (React = a JavaScript library for building web pages. Tailwind CSS = a set of ready-made style names that make pages look good quickly.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) The page runs on my laptop, shows a styled heading, and a button that changes the text when clicked.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: PostgreSQL basics
User story: As a team member, I want to create a table and save and read rows in PostgreSQL, so that I understand how our app stores data. (PostgreSQL = a free database, an organised place to store data. SQL = the language used to talk to a database.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I created a "tasks" table, saved 3 rows and read them back with SQL.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Docker basics
User story: As a team member, I want to run a small program in a Docker container, so that my code runs the same way on every teammate's laptop. (Docker = a tool that packs a program with everything it needs into a container.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) A hello container starts with one command and shows its message.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: pytest basics
User story: As a team member, I want to write simple automatic tests with pytest, so that I can check my code without testing by hand. (pytest = a Python tool that runs small test programs which check our code.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I wrote 2 passing tests, and I showed one failing test and then fixed it.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Password hashing basics (bcrypt or Argon2)
User story: As a team member, I want to hash and check a password in a small example, so that I understand how to store passwords safely. (Hashing = turning a password into a scrambled code that cannot be turned back. bcrypt and Argon2 = free tools that do this safely.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) My example accepts the right password and rejects a wrong one, and hashing the same password twice gives two different codes.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Walking skeleton: one task from the web page to the database and back
User story: As a user planning my week, I want to add one Personal task and see it on my screen, so that I know the app saves what I type. (A walking skeleton = the smallest version that works from start to finish. It is a first, simple path through the whole system.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) The React page sends the task to the FastAPI backend and it is saved in PostgreSQL.
2) After I refresh the page, the saved task is still shown.
3) The whole thing starts with one documented command (Docker if the laptop can run it, otherwise a run script) and was merged by pull request.
Suggested sprint: 3 (may start in 2 if the learning finishes early)

Title: Sign-up and login with hashed passwords and login attempt limits
User story: As a user with Personal and Work tasks, I want to sign up and log in with a password, so that only I can see my tasks and events.
Acceptance criteria:
1) The database stores a hash, never the plain password.
2) After 5 wrong passwords in a row the account is locked for a short time.
3) A pytest test checks that a right password works and a wrong one fails.

Title: In-app calendar with the six categories and event status
User story: As a user with a full life, I want a calendar where each event has a category (Study, Work, Personal, Family, Health or Errands), so that I can see all of my life in one place.
Acceptance criteria:
1) I can add an event with a title, a time and one of the six categories.
2) The calendar shows each event with its category.
3) Each event stores whether it was kept, moved or missed.

Title: Every member has a working setup
User story: As a team member, I want my laptop to have all the tools we need installed and checked, so that I can start the learning items in Sprint 2 without losing time. (Git = the tool that records changes to code; a commit is one saved set of changes. Python = the programming language of our backend. Node.js = a tool that lets a laptop run JavaScript, which React needs. npm = the tool that installs JavaScript packages. pgAdmin = a free window for looking at a PostgreSQL database.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) git --version, python --version, node --version and npm --version each show a version number, and I posted one screenshot of these checks in the team group.
2) My commits show my own name and GitHub email.
3) For PostgreSQL and Docker, either pgAdmin opens and docker --version works, or I told the team why my laptop cannot run them.

Title: Delete my data: a user can delete their account and all their data
User story: As a user with Family and Health events, I want to delete my account and all my data, so that nothing about my life stays stored if I stop using the app.
Acceptance criteria:
1) A "Delete my account" button asks for my password and then removes my account.
2) After deleting, my tasks, events and categories are no longer in the database (checked by looking in the database).
3) A pytest test shows that another user's data is still there.

Title: Private categories: a user can lock a category so other accounts cannot read it and it is never sent to the AI
User story: As a user with Health and Family events, I want to lock a category, so that other accounts cannot read it and its text is never sent to the AI.
Acceptance criteria:
1) I can lock and unlock any of the six categories.
2) A second test account cannot see the events in my locked category.
3) Text from a locked category is never sent to the AI (checked in the test log, using fake data).

Title: Report a bad answer button for the coach
User story: As a user studying for an exam, I want to report a bad coach answer with one click, so that wrong hints are found and fixed.
Acceptance criteria:
1) Every coach answer has a "Report a bad answer" button.
2) Clicking it saves the question, the answer and the time, with no personal details.
3) The team can see the list of reports.

Title: Export the calendar as a file
User story: As a user with a busy week, I want to download my calendar as a file, so that I can open it in another calendar app. (The usual calendar file type is called .ics.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) An "Export" button downloads a calendar file.
2) The file contains my events with their title, time and category.
3) The file opens without errors in one free calendar app that we test with.

Title: Protect the learning data from fake events: rate limits, outlier filter and a tampering test
User story: As a user who relies on time suggestions, I want protection against fake events that could mislead the learning, so that my suggestions stay trustworthy. (A rate limit = a limit on how many requests one account can make in a short time. An outlier = a value far away from all the others, such as 50 events at 3 a.m. A tampering test = a test where we try to fool our own app on purpose.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) One account cannot add more than 20 new events in one minute (the number is a guess the team can change).
2) The outlier filter ignores events that are far outside normal when the model learns.
3) A tampering test adds bulk fake events to a test account, and the suggestions change only a little (before and after are written down).

Title: Compare free AI options and choose one (cost check)
User story: As a team member, I want to compare free AI options and choose one, so that our coach and chat do not cost money and we know the limits before the Sprint 3 work needs them. (A free option usually has limits, such as how many questions you can ask per day.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note compares at least 3 free AI options (what is free, the limits, how private it is) and is saved in our "learning" folder.
2) The team chose one option and wrote the reason in one line, and one small test question got an answer from it.
3) I explained the choice in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.
